title: No, Mark Zuckerberg, the future is not (yet) for everyone
gist: A Southeast Asian rejoinder to Mark Zuckerberg's 'The Future Is for Everyone' essay: distributing superintelligence via a private corporation like Meta may expand users' capabilities while entrenching Meta's power, and 'access' is a material and institutional condition — uneven infrastructure, chip/energy control and cultural representation mean broad AI access is neither simple nor inherently beneficial.

insights.claim: The authors argue Zuckerberg's superintelligence vision rests on two unexamined assumptions — that 'everyone' is a population to whom access can simply be provisioned, and that broad access to superintelligence is inherently beneficial to humanity.
insights.speaker: Karryl Kim Sagun Trajano
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI-democratisation narrative as contestable — a critical lens for evaluating Big Tech's 'AI for everyone' positioning.
insights.quote: that “everyone” is a population for whom access can simply be provisioned, and that broad access to superintelligence is inherently beneficial to humanity
insights.locator: But the argument rests on two unexamined assumptions

insights.claim: The authors contend that distributing powerful AI through a private corporation does not decentralise power — if Meta distributes AI to individuals it may expand their capabilities while simultaneously strengthening Meta's institutional power, market position and control over the technology.
insights.speaker: Karryl Kim Sagun Trajano
insights.so_what: The 'democratisation strengthens the platform' argument is a warning that Meta's AI giveaway is also a market-entrenchment strategy.
insights.quote: Widespread access to Meta’s AI is not necessarily the same as democratising superintelligence.
insights.locator: Zuckerberg also argues that distributing superintelligence

insights.claim: In 2015 Zuckerberg defended subsidised Facebook access in developing countries as supporting social and economic rights, but the main benefactor was Facebook (Meta) expanding into new markets.
insights.speaker: Karryl Kim Sagun Trajano
insights.so_what: Precedent that Meta's 'access for all' framing has historically served Meta's expansion — grounds for scepticism toward the AI version.
insights.locator: In 2015, he defended subsidised Facebook access

insights.claim: In Myanmar, Facebook's amplification and failure to moderate harmful content were linked by UN investigators to conditions in which violence could scale, and in the Philippines Facebook was used to amplify election disinformation during the 2022 elections.
insights.speaker: Karryl Kim Sagun Trajano
insights.so_what: Concrete harm precedents show rapid poorly-moderated platform expansion can scale harm — the risk the authors say AI provisioning repeats.

themes.theme: Access as material and institutional condition

insights.claim: The authors argue access is a material and institutional condition, not a product feature: Southeast Asia is highly uneven, with Singapore ranking among the world's strongest governments for AI readiness while capability gaps across ASEAN persist in connectivity, digital skills and innovation networks.
insights.speaker: Karryl Kim Sagun Trajano
insights.so_what: Frames AI access as gated by infrastructure and institutions, not price — a corrective for optimistic AI-diffusion assumptions in emerging markets.
insights.quote: Access is a material and institutional condition, not simply a product feature.
insights.locator: Southeast Asia demonstrates why this is not enough

insights.claim: The authors argue access to superintelligence will depend not only on price but on who controls the chips, energy and infrastructure behind it, with US-China semiconductor controls reshaping regional supply chains and Southeast Asian countries competing for data-centre and AI investment.
insights.speaker: Karryl Kim Sagun Trajano
insights.so_what: Ties AI access to the chip/energy/data-centre supply chain and US-China controls — the real chokepoints for AI diffusion.
insights.quote: Access to superintelligence will depend not only on price, but on who controls the chips, energy, and infrastructure behind it.
insights.locator: US–China semiconductor controls are also reshaping

insights.claim: The authors note AI can be widely accessible while still reflecting the assumptions, languages and priorities of the societies where its data and development are concentrated, so distribution without representation risks making AI more accessible without making it more locally relevant.
insights.speaker: Karryl Kim Sagun Trajano
insights.so_what: Flags a market gap for locally grounded models over generic Silicon Valley AI in linguistically diverse regions.
insights.quote: Distribution without representation risks making AI more accessible without making it more locally relevant.

insights.claim: The authors cite Singapore's SEA-LION large language model, developed around Southeast Asian languages and cultural contexts, as an example of what more locally grounded AI development can look like.
insights.speaker: Karryl Kim Sagun Trajano
insights.so_what: Points to regionally-developed models as the alternative to dependence on US-centric AI — a signal for sovereign-AI investment themes.
insights.locator: Large language models such as Singapore’s SEA-LION
